Q1 2025 Medtech VC and PE Trends
VC and PE activity
VC activity
There are clear signs of momentum for medical technology (medtech) VC investment. In Q1, 
VC funding totaled $4.1 billion, the highest figure since Q1 2022. The quarterly deal count also 
reversed a four-quarter decline by reaching 216 confirmed transactions—and this is likely an 
undercount, as we expect additional deals to be reported for the quarter. Preliminary data for Q2 
shows over $3 billion of VC funding in the sector so far, with Neuralink’s $650 million deal leading 
the way. 2025 is shaping up to be a strong year for global medtech funding, especially compared 
with the funding doldrums of the past few years. 
In Q1, 11 deals met or exceeded the $100 million mark, the highest being Sweden-based 
whole-body-imaging startup Neko Health’s $260 million Series B. EverBridge Medical claimed the 
second spot, raising $138.9 million. Neko’s whole-body-screening peer Prenuvo was also among 
the top deals with a $120 million Series B. It has been an active start to the year for the burgeoning 
whole-body-screening subsector, which we explored in prior research; on May 5, Function 
Health acquired Ezra, integrating Ezra’s whole-body-scanning services into Function Health’s 
subscription-based diagnostic platform.
Following a challenging stretch for the broader consumer health space, the medtech sector is 
showing renewed momentum as the lines continue to blur between medtech and traditional digital 
health offerings. This convergence is exemplified by the growing adoption of smart rings (such as 
Oura and WHOOP), consumer-grade glucose monitors, and longevity-focused platforms such as 
Superpower and the aforementioned Function Health.
PE activity
PE deal activity in the medtech sector is off to a solid start in 2025, with 44 deals already 
completed in Q1—well ahead of the pace set in 2024, which saw 126 PE transactions during the 
year. Notably, PE firms participated in Saluda Medical’s $100 million funding round in January, 
including TPG and Redmile Group, bringing the neuromodulation startup’s fundraising total to over 
$600 million to date. In a previous report, we noted that organ transplant technology remains an 
underrated funding category, and recent developments have underscored this view, including last 
year’s acquisition of VC-backed Paragonix Technologies and PE-backed OrganOx securing $142 
million in development capital from a diverse mix of PE and VC investors in February.
Despite solid fundraising momentum, PE exits have been scarce in the medtech sector—a notable 
contrast to the rising pace of PE exits seen in other areas of healthcare, particularly pharma 
services and healthcare services, where M&A has rebounded. Looking ahead, PE-backed Caris Life 
Sciences filed for an IPO on May 23 and will be the latest medtech company heading toward the 
public markets as it seeks to raise over $400 million at a $5.3 billion valuation.1 Medline Industries 
also remains on our IPO watchlist this year, a potential bellwether for larger-scale PE-backed 
medtech exits.
1: “Sixth Street-Backed Caris Life Sciences Targets $5.3 Billion Valuation in US IPO,” Reuters, Arasu Kannagi Basil, June 9, 2025.

Exit outlook
There were no significant medtech VC exits in the first quarter, and the total exit value remained 
roughly in line with the previous two quarters. Large exits continue to be rare, with overall exit 
value in recent years heavily dependent on major transactions and listings, such as Tempus AI’s 
IPO in June 2024 and the $6 billion acquisition of Athelas by Commure in October 2023. Still, the 
first quarter featured three notable exits in the sector: the acquisitions of SoniVie and Gynesonics 
for $600 million and $350 million, respectively, and Beta Bionics’ public listing. The latter was part 
of a wave of small-cap medtech IPOs last year, including listings by Kestra Medical Technologies 
and Ceribell. While these listings were solid outcomes for the companies’ investors, all three 
companies currently trade at or below a $1 billion market cap and were not among the most highly 
valued medtech startups at their time of listing.
On the M&A front, corporate spin-offs are not entirely out of favor: In February, BD announced it 
would spin off its diagnostic and biosciences businesses, and in May, Medtronic said it would spin 
off its diabetes business within the next 18 months. These moves reflect a continued focus by large 
strategics on core operations, though they are not without scrutiny: Medtronic’s diabetes spin-off 
raised eyebrows among some analysts given its healthy performance and market positioning.2
Boston Scientific remains an active leader in medtech M&A, exemplified by its acquisition of 
SoniVie to bolster its presence in the emerging renal denervation space. However, our earlier 
thesis that the new US presidential administration’s more lenient regulatory stance would catalyze 
M&A activity has yet to play out, as broader market turbulence in early 2025 has complicated 
dealmaking conditions across sectors. Additionally, regulatory resistance remains a headwind: The 
Federal Trade Commission is continuing its legal challenge of the $627 million PE acquisition of 
Surmodics, a case now backed by the attorneys general of Illinois and Minnesota.
Regulatory update
The regulatory and reimbursement climate remains in flux, with near-term uncertainty posing 
challenges for long-term capital planning across the medtech sector. In a recent BTIG survey of 30 
hospital purchasing leaders, two-thirds of respondents anticipated reduced capital budgets if the 
Medicaid cuts outlined in the House version of the bill proceed—an outcome that could impact the 
procurement of high-ticket devices such as robotic systems and imaging platforms.3 Meanwhile, 
the Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA’s) decision not to appeal the court ruling that blocked 
the Biden administration’s final rule on lab-developed tests (LDTs) halts efforts to expand federal 
oversight in this space. This effectively preserves the status quo, with thousands of diagnostic 
assays continuing to operate under minimal FDA scrutiny. For diagnostics investors—and 
particularly those backing LDT-heavy platforms—this outcome is mixed: It maintains accelerated 
commercial pathways, but the absence of formal regulation could pose a modest headwind to 
long-term adoption given the continued lower barriers to entry for new tests.
